evals.query: How do I enable Kora's resilience features (retry, circuit breaker, timeout) in my application?
expected_behavior: Adds implementation "io.koraframework:resilient-kora"
Adds the mandatory processor: Java annotationProcessor "io.koraframework:annotation-processors", Kotlin ksp "io.koraframework:symbol-processors"
Uses platform "io.koraframework:kora-bom" at 2.0.0.RC2 (koraVersion property) from plain mavenCentral(), without pinning per-artifact versions
Has the @KoraApp interface extend io.koraframework.resilient.ResilientModule
States that the generated $<Spec>_Module must NOT be extended manually — @KoraApp picks it up
anti_behavior: Writes ru.tinkoff.kora:resilient-kora or the ru.tinkoff.kora:kora-parent BOM
Pins 2.0.0-SNAPSHOT or 2.0.0.alpha6 as the version for a new project
Adds the generated spec module to the @KoraApp extends list

evals.query: My Kora build fails with: error: incompatible types: String cannot be converted to Class<? extends Timeouter>. The line is @Timeout("pet") on PetService.findById. What is wrong?
expected_behavior: Identifies this as un-migrated Kora 1.x code: in 2.0 the annotation attribute is Class<? extends Timeouter>, not String
Declares a spec interface annotated @TimeoutSpec("resilient.timeout.pet") that extends io.koraframework.resilient.timeout.Timeouter
Changes the method annotation to @Timeout(PetTimeouter.class)
Notes that the runtime contract is spelled Timeouter while Timeout is the annotation
Keeps the existing resilient.timeout.pet config section rather than renaming it
anti_behavior: Suggests casting, changing the string, or suppressing the error
Claims io.koraframework provides a ready-made DefaultTimeouter or PetTimeouter type
Recommends a blind find/replace across the codebase as the whole migration

evals.query: After bumping our Kotlin Kora service to 2.0, KSP crashes with java.lang.ClassCastException: class java.lang.String cannot be cast to class com.google.devtools.ksp.symbol.KSType and the stack trace only names Kora classes. How do I find the cause?
expected_behavior: Explains that the Kora resilient symbol processor reads the annotation value with a checked cast to KSType, so a leftover string argument crashes it instead of producing a readable diagnostic
Tells the user to search for the string forms @Retryable(", @CircuitBreakable(", @Timeout(", @RateLimited("
Replaces each with a spec interface: @RetrySpec("...") interface X : Retry, then @Retryable(X::class)
Notes the equivalent Java symptom is a plain compile error about String not converting to Class<? extends ...>
anti_behavior: Blames KSP version, Kotlin version, or the Gradle cache as the root cause
Suggests disabling KSP or the resilient processor
Cites a Kora migration document that is not shipped with this package as if it were authoritative

evals.query: I ported this circuit breaker config to Kora 2.0: resilient.circuitbreaker.order { slidingWindowSize = 50, minimumRequiredCalls = 25, failureRateThreshold = 50, waitDurationInOpenState = "30s", permittedCallsInHalfOpenState = 5 }. The app builds but dies on startup. Why?
expected_behavior: Identifies that slidingWindowSize no longer exists and is silently ignored as an unknown HOCON key
Replaces it with a countBased.windowSize = 50 block plus an explicit type

States the failure is an IllegalArgumentException during graph initialisation — "CircuitBreaker '<Spec>' property 'countBased' is not configured" — not a config-validation error and not a compile error
Notes the countBased block is required for STRIPED_APPROX (the default), FIXED_WINDOW and RING_BUFFER; TIME_BASED needs a timeBased block instead
Mentions RING_BUFFER is the closest match to the 1.x counting window while the migrated examples use FIXED_WINDOW
anti_behavior: Says the app fails with an NPE
Claims countBased is optional because the config accessor is @Nullable
Keeps slidingWindowSize anywhere in the output
Invents a minimumNumberOfCalls key

evals.query: In Kora 1.x our config had resilient.circuitbreaker.default with all the settings and resilient.circuitbreaker.payment overriding just failureRateThreshold = 30. I kept both in 2.0 and pointed @CircuitBreakerSpec at resilient.circuitbreaker.payment. Is that still equivalent?
expected_behavior: States it is not equivalent: in 2.0 a spec resolves exactly one config path and named sections do not merge with `default`
Explains that unset keys fall back to the config type's defaults, not to the neighbouring section
Points out that failureRateThreshold, minimumRequiredCalls, waitDurationInOpenState and permittedCallsInHalfOpenState have no defaults at all, so the partial section fails to start
Fills the payment section completely, including a window type and countBased.windowSize
Notes the default section becomes dead config once nothing points at it and should be removed or given its own spec
anti_behavior: Claims 2.0 still merges a named section with `default`
Suggests a HOCON include or ${resilient.circuitbreaker.default} substitution as the documented Kora mechanism without flagging it as the user's own workaround
Leaves the partially-filled section as correct

evals.query: Our circuit breaker trips on HTTP 404s. In Kora 1.x we had a CircuitBreakerPredicate with name() returning "IgnoreBusinessErrors" and wired it with failurePredicateName in the config. Port it to 2.0 so only 5xx counts.
expected_behavior: Removes the failurePredicateName config key entirely — it no longer selects anything in 2.0
Implements io.koraframework.resilient.circuitbreaker.CircuitBreakerPredicate with the single method isCircuitBreakerFailure(Throwable) and no name() method
Registers it as a @Component annotated @Tag(<CircuitBreakerSpec class>.class) — the tag is the only wiring
Inspects the response code (HttpClientResponseException.getCode()) to keep only 5xx as failures
Mentions the alternative of overriding isFailure(Throwable) as a default method on the spec interface, and that a tagged predicate overrides it
anti_behavior: Keeps name() or test(Throwable) on the predicate
Keeps or reintroduces a failurePredicateName config key
Registers the predicate as a plain untagged @Component and claims it will be picked up
Uses a non-Kora resilience predicate API

evals.query: This does not compile after upgrading to Kora 2.0: @Fallback(value = "product.read", method = "getFromCache(id)"). We also have a resilient.fallback."product.read" section with a failurePredicateName. What is the 2.0 equivalent?
expected_behavior: States the value attribute was removed — @Fallback(method = "getFromCache(id)") is the only form
States there is no @FallbackSpec, no resilient.fallback.<name> config section and no FallbackPredicate in 2.0
Deletes the resilient.fallback."product.read" section, noting only resilient.telemetry.fallback survives
Replaces the predicate with a @Fallback.Reason parameter on the fallback method, explaining that its declared type filters which exceptions trigger the fallback
Notes the reason parameter is not named inside the method reference string
anti_behavior: Keeps @Fallback(value = ...)
Invents a @FallbackSpec annotation or a FallbackSpec interface
Keeps a resilient.fallback.<name> configuration section
Claims FallbackPredicate still exists

evals.query: I am migrating a Kotlin service where OrderService.load, OrderService.refresh and OrderAdminService.reload all had @CircuitBreaker("order"). Should I create a spec interface per method?
expected_behavior: Says no: one spec interface per logical configuration name, shared by all three methods across both classes

Explains that the spec interface is the circuit breaker's identity, so duplicate interfaces on the same config path create independent breakers with independent windows and state — they would never trip together

Produces a single @CircuitBreakerSpec("resilient.circuitbreaker.order") interface OrderCircuitBreaker : CircuitBreaker and annotates all three methods with @CircuitBreakable(OrderCircuitBreaker::class)
Reminds that in Kotlin both classes and all three methods must be open
anti_behavior: Creates one spec interface per method or per class
Claims two interfaces on the same config path share one runtime instance
Suggests distinguishing them with @Tag on the annotated methods

evals.query: I added @Retryable(UserRetry::class) to a Kotlin class method and the build fails with "AOP aspect cannot be applied to class 'com.example.UserService' because the class is not open". What do I do?
expected_behavior: Marks the class open and the annotated method open — both are required for the generated $UserService__AopProxy subclass
Notes this is a hard compile error in Kora 2.0, not a silently skipped aspect
Mentions the companion error for a non-open function: "AOP aspect cannot be applied to function ... because the function is not open"
Notes the Java equivalent is "AOP aspect cannot be applied to class ... because the class is final"
anti_behavior: Suggests the all-open Kotlin compiler plugin as the Kora-documented solution
Claims the aspect would just be skipped silently
Suggests making the class an interface or adding a runtime proxy

evals.query: Wrap a payment charge call in Kora 2.0 with a per-attempt timeout, retry on transient failures, a circuit breaker, and a fallback for graceful degradation.
expected_behavior: Declares one spec interface per aspect: @CircuitBreakerSpec, @RetrySpec and @TimeoutSpec on interfaces extending CircuitBreaker, Retry and Timeouter
Stacks @Fallback first (outermost), then @CircuitBreakable, then @Retryable, then @Timeout last (innermost) on one @Component method, and states that declaration order is nesting order
Explains the per-attempt bound follows from @Timeout being inside @Retryable, and that swapping them makes the timeout a budget for the whole chain
Adds a same-class protected fallback method whose parameters match the method reference exactly
Provides resilient.* config for all three specs, with the circuit-breaker section including a type and countBased.windowSize
anti_behavior: Uses string-named annotations such as @CircuitBreaker("payment") or @Retry("payment")
Passes a value attribute to @Fallback
Puts @Fallback last, which would swallow failures before the circuit breaker records them
Introduces Resilience4j or another external resilience library

evals.query: I cannot annotate the method I need to protect, and in Kora 1.x I used CircuitBreakerManager.get("order"). How do I use a circuit breaker imperatively in Kora 2.0?
expected_behavior: States that CircuitBreakerManager, RetryManager, TimeoutManager and FallbackManager do not exist in Kora 2.0
Injects the spec interface itself by constructor — the generated module registers it as a graph component
Calls the CircuitBreaker contract directly: accept(callable), accept(callable, fallback), or tryAcquire()/acquire() paired with releaseOnSuccess()/releaseOnError(t)
Notes the same pattern applies to Retry (retry(...)), Timeouter (execute(...)) and RateLimiter (tryAcquire()/acquire())
anti_behavior: Uses any *Manager type or a name-based lookup
Injects the generated $<Spec>_Impl class instead of the spec interface
Constructs a KoraCircuitBreaker by hand

evals.query: Configure a Kora 2.0 retry for an external API: exponential backoff starting at 100ms, capped at 5s, with jitter, retrying at most 4 times, and only on connection-level failures.
expected_behavior: Declares a @RetrySpec interface extending Retry and applies @Retryable(<Spec>.class)
Sets attempts = 4 and notes that attempts counts retries, so up to 5 invocations happen
Uses a backoff block (multiplier, delayMax) and states it replaces delayStep rather than combining with it
Adds a jitter block with type = FULL
Restricts the exceptions with a @Tag(<Spec>.class) @Component implementing RetryPredicate.isRetryFailure(Throwable), not a failurePredicateName key
Notes a rejected exception propagates unchanged instead of becoming RetryExhaustedException
anti_behavior: Uses failurePredicateName or a RetryPredicate with name()/test()
Claims delayStep produces exponential backoff
Says attempts is the total number of invocations
Uses @Retry("external")

evals.query: Write a @KoraAppTest that proves our circuit breaker opens after two failures, overriding the resilience config inside the test.
expected_behavior: Implements KoraAppTestConfigModifier and returns KoraConfigModification.ofString("""...""") with the resilient block
Includes the window block in the embedded HOCON — a type plus countBased.windowSize — and all required circuit-breaker keys, or the graph fails to initialise
Tunes the values down (small windowSize, minimumRequiredCalls of 1-2, failureRateThreshold = 100, sub-second waitDurationInOpenState) so the breaker trips within a few calls
Injects the service with @TestComponent and asserts on invocation counts against a fake collaborator rather than on wall-clock timing
Notes that CallNotPermittedException is what an OPEN breaker throws
anti_behavior: Omits the countBased block from the embedded test HOCON
Assumes the test picks up resilient.circuitbreaker.default automatically
Mocks the circuit breaker instead of exercising the real graph
Uses Thread.sleep-based timing as the assertion

evals.query: I need to cap outbound SMS notifications at 100 per second in our Kora 2.0 service, shared between two sender classes.
expected_behavior: Uses @RateLimited with a @RateLimiterSpec interface extending io.koraframework.resilient.ratelimiter.RateLimiter, noting it is new in 2.0
Declares a single spec interface used by both classes so they share one permit pool
Configures limitForPeriod = 100 and limitRefreshPeriod = "1s", both required
States that an exceeded limit throws RateLimitExceededException immediately — callers are never blocked or queued

Notes it is a per-process limiter whose default algorithm is TOKEN_BUCKET (GCRA, burst up to limitForPeriod), with type = FIXED_WINDOW as the alternative, and points to @RateLimiterDistributedSpec when the quota must hold across instances
anti_behavior: Claims @RateLimited existed in Kora 1.x
Describes the limiter as blocking or queueing callers
Gives each class its own spec interface on the same config path
Suggests a resilient.ratelimiter key set other than limitForPeriod / limitRefreshPeriod / type / enabled
Claims KoraRateLimiter is fixed-window only or not a token bucket

evals.query: Our Kora 2.0 service uses @CircuitBreakable and @Retryable but no resilient.* metrics show up in Prometheus and there is nothing in the logs either. Everything else reports fine.
expected_behavior: States that resilient telemetry is off by default — logging, metrics and tracing all default to false for the resilience aspects
Enables it under resilient.telemetry.<aspect> (circuitBreaker, retry, timeout, fallback, rateLimiter), or per spec under <specPath>.telemetry
Points out the camelCase spelling of the resilient.telemetry sub-keys
Names the real metric families, e.g. resilient.circuitbreaker.state, resilient.circuitbreaker.transition, resilient.retry.attempts, resilient.retry.exhausted
Notes that metrics also require the micrometer module in the graph
anti_behavior: Claims resilience metrics are enabled by default
Only raises the logger level and stops there
Invents metric names not emitted by resilient-kora

evals.query: Our Kora 1.x service had @CircuitBreaker("catalog") on a method returning Mono<Catalog>, and a Kotlin one on a suspend fun. What happens to both in 2.0?
expected_behavior: States that Mono/Flux are gone as Kora contracts in 2.0 and no resilience aspect accepts a Publisher return type — the build fails with "cannot be applied ... because return type ... is not supported by this aspect"
Rewrites the reactive method to a synchronous signature, noting Kora 2.0 contracts are synchronous on virtual threads
States that Kotlin suspend and Flow ARE supported by the resilience aspects, so the suspend fun keeps working once the annotation is retyped to a spec class
Notes that in Kotlin CompletionStage/CompletableFuture are rejected by every resilience aspect, while Java accepts them for all aspects except @RateLimited
anti_behavior: Suggests adding reactor-core to keep Mono/Flux working with Kora aspects
Claims Kotlin suspend functions are unsupported by the resilience aspects
Leaves a Mono/Flux signature in the output

evals.query: Our Kora 2.0 @RateLimited limiter is set to limitForPeriod = 100, limitRefreshPeriod = "1s". Someone on the team says it lets 200 calls through around a second boundary because it is a fixed window. Is that right, and how do I choose the algorithm?
expected_behavior: States that the local limiter selects its algorithm with the `type` key (RateLimiterConfig.type, enum RateLimiterType) and that the default is TOKEN_BUCKET
Explains TOKEN_BUCKET is GCRA: continuous refill at limitForPeriod / limitRefreshPeriod with a burst of up to limitForPeriod after idle, so it does not double at a window boundary
Explains that only type = FIXED_WINDOW has the up-to-2x boundary behaviour, and when a literal quota per window is worth that
States that both algorithms reject immediately with RateLimitExceededException and never block or queue
anti_behavior: Claims KoraRateLimiter is fixed-window only or 'not a token bucket'
Recommends halving limitRefreshPeriod as the only fix for boundary bursts
Invents keys such as algorithm, burst or timeoutDuration for the local @RateLimiterSpec section
Claims the token bucket waits for a permit

evals.query: In Kora 2.0 I don't want @Retryable to retry our ValidationException, and I don't want our circuit breaker to count OrderNotFoundException as a failure. Is there something simpler than writing predicates?
expected_behavior: Uses the marker interfaces io.koraframework.resilient.retry.NonRetryableException and io.koraframework.resilient.circuitbreaker.NonCircuitableException
Notes both are interfaces, so the exceptions keep their superclass and add the marker to implements (Kotlin: to the supertype list)
States a NonRetryableException propagates on the first throw without RetryExhaustedException
States a NonCircuitableException still propagates to the caller but is counted as neither a failure nor a success by the breaker
Warns that a tagged RetryPredicate/CircuitBreakerPredicate or an overridden isFailure replaces the default check, so the markers are only honoured by the default isFailure
anti_behavior: Invents annotations such as @NonRetryable or @NoRetry
Declares NonRetryableException or NonCircuitableException as a class to extend
Places the markers in io.koraframework.resilient.exception or another wrong package
Claims the markers still apply when a tagged predicate is present

evals.query: Our Kora 2.0 service has ten @RetrySpec retries. For just one of them, PricingRetry, I want a different retry budget implementation than the one built from config. How is the retry budget wired?
expected_behavior: Explains the RetryBudget interface (tryAcquireRetryToken, onSuccess, availableTokens) with KoraRetryBudget as the in-JVM implementation
Explains that each retry gets its budget from a RetryBudgetFactory: a factory tagged @Tag(PricingRetry.class) wins for that retry, else the untagged one

States the untagged default is DefaultRetryBudgetFactory from ResilientModule, which builds a KoraRetryBudget from the retryBudget block and returns null (no budget) when the block is absent or disabled
Registers a RetryBudgetFactory component tagged @Tag(PricingRetry.class), e.g. in a @Module, and notes an untagged one would replace the default for every retry
Notes that a denied token propagates the original exception and tags resilient.retry.exhausted with resilient.reason=EXHAUSTED_BUDGET
anti_behavior: Invents a config key such as retryBudget.type or retryBudgetFactoryName to pick the implementation
Uses a string name or failurePredicateName-style lookup
Claims the retry budget is shared across service instances by default

evals.query: We run six replicas of a Kora 2.0 service and the partner API allows 50 requests per second in total, not per replica. We already use Redis. How do I rate limit across all replicas?
expected_behavior: Adds io.koraframework:resilient-kora-distributed-redis-lettuce (which brings resilient-kora-distributed and redis-lettuce) and extends LettuceDistributedResilientModule on the @KoraApp while keeping ResilientModule

Declares the spec with @RateLimiterDistributedSpec("...") from io.koraframework.resilient.distributed.ratelimiter.annotation on an interface extending io.koraframework.resilient.ratelimiter.RateLimiter, and keeps using @RateLimited(Spec.class)
Configures limitForPeriod, limitRefreshPeriod and the required keyPrefix, and notes the algorithm key is `algorithm` (TOKEN_BUCKET default, or FIXED_WINDOW), not `type`
Configures the Redis connection through the lettuce section (lettuce.uri; standalone or cluster)
States that a Redis failure propagates as an exception rather than letting the call through
anti_behavior: Keeps @RateLimiterSpec and claims its state is shared between replicas
Divides the limit by the replica count as the recommended solution
Writes a Lua script or a custom Redis client as a required step
Uses `type = TOKEN_BUCKET` inside the distributed section

evals.query: Can Kora 2.0's distributed rate limiter limit each tenant separately, e.g. 10 requests per second per tenantId, using DistributedRateLimiterFactory?
expected_behavior: States that the framework source has no DistributedRateLimiterFactory and no per-key limiter: a @RateLimiterDistributedSpec maps to one Redis key, <keyPrefix>:<SpecSimpleName>
Says per-tenant limiting has to be implemented in application code
Warns that specs with the same simple name and keyPrefix share one quota across services
anti_behavior: Shows DistributedRateLimiterFactory.get(key) or any other per-key API as if it existed
Claims a SpEL/placeholder in the spec path creates one limiter per tenant

evals.query: Make the retry budget of PartnerRetry shared across all instances of our Kora 2.0 service via Redis.
expected_behavior: Uses io.koraframework.resilient.distributed.retry.DistributedRetryBudgetFactory built from the DistributedRetryBudgetClient supplied by LettuceDistributedResilientModule
Registers it as a RetryBudgetFactory component tagged @Tag(PartnerRetry.class), noting it is not registered by any module automatically
Keeps the retryBudget block on resilient.retry.partner because the distributed factory returns no budget without it
Notes minTokensPerSecond is ignored by the distributed budget and that the key is <keyPrefix>:PartnerRetry with a TTL (default prefix kora:retrybudget, 10 minutes)
anti_behavior: Injects DistributedRetryBudgetFactory as if a module provided it
Invents a retryBudget.distributed or retryBudget.redis config key
Drops the retryBudget block

evals.query: How can I log the current state of a Kora 2.0 circuit breaker and rate limiter from my code while debugging?
expected_behavior: Injects the spec interface and logs its toString(), which reports the implementation and live state (breaker state and counters, available permits; retries and retry budgets likewise)
Says the toString format is for humans and should not be parsed
Mentions resilient.circuitbreaker.state as the metric to monitor state in production, with telemetry enabled explicitly
anti_behavior: Calls a getState() method on the CircuitBreaker contract
Uses a CircuitBreakerManager or RateLimiterManager

evals.query: Write a PromQL alert for Kora 2.0 when the circuit breaker configured at resilient.circuitbreaker.payments is OPEN, and a panel for rejected rate-limiter acquires.
expected_behavior: Enables metrics first (resilient.telemetry.circuitBreaker / rateLimiter or <specPath>.telemetry, off by default) and needs MetricsModule in the graph
Uses resilient_circuitbreaker_state == 2 (0 CLOSED, 1 HALF_OPEN, 2 OPEN) filtered by the resilient_name label equal to the spec's config path
Uses resilient_ratelimiter_acquire with resilient_status="rejected"
States that since 2.0.0.RC2 every resilience tag is resilient.-prefixed (resilient.name, resilient.state, resilient.status, resilient.reason, resilient.type)
anti_behavior: Filters on a bare name="..." or status="..." label (the RC1 tag names)
